title: Karmic tail 6-8-20 in the destiny matrix: “Family Disappointment”, the family court and a calling without a verdict

seo.title: Karmic Tail 6-8-20 “Family Disappointment” in the Destiny Matrix
seo.description: 6-8-20: every choice of the heart goes before a family court. A ten-second date check, why one child in twenty born since 2000 has it, and Waite’s word “disgrace”.

short: 6-8-20 is the karmic tail that popular readings of the destiny matrix call “Family Disappointment” (less often, “Family Disgrace”). Its script: every important choice of the heart — whom to love, where to live, what to do for a living, how to raise children — the person lives through as a case heard in a family court. Will they be proud or ashamed? Will they accept it or turn away? The entry into the circle is the Lovers (6): a choice that concerns more than just you. The circle is held by Strength (8): the choice is held by force — either you swallow your desire and stay the family’s pride, or you defend it against everyone and become an outcast. (In many calculators the eight is Justice, and then the circle is held by a family ledger: who owes whom what. More on this below.) At the root stands Judgement (20) — in Russian simply Sud, “the court” — but not as a verdict: as a call that the person hears for themselves. So the main question of this tail is not “how not to disappoint my family” and not “how to break free of them” but how to choose what is yours without cutting the bond. Everyone with 6-8-20 has a hidden fourth card — the Emperor in the centre of the matrix. And this is a young tail: among people born in the 1930s it went to one person in 126, and among children born after 2000 it goes to one in twenty.

sections.h2: Do you have the 6-8-20 tail: a ten-second check
paragraphs: The tail depends entirely on one number — the sum of the first three arcana of the matrix. For 6-8-20 the rule could not be simpler: the sum must be exactly 20.

ol: **Day arcanum** — the day you were born. If it is over 22, add its digits: 25 → 7, 28 → 10, 31 → 4.
**Year arcanum** — the sum of the digits of the year. If it comes out over 22, add the digits again: 1986 → 24 → 6, while 1970 → 17.

paragraphs: Add up the three numbers. If you get **20**, you have 6-8-20. There are no other options.

ul: 05.07.2000: 5 + 7 + 2 = 14 → not this one. This is 6-20-14: the same entry, Judgement in the middle, but a different root.
31.03.1993: 4 + 3 + 22 = 29 → not this one. This is 15-8-11: the same centre and the same Strength in the middle, but a different entry and root.

paragraphs: Why it works. A sum of 20 puts D = 20 in the bottom corner of the chart. The centre E = 20 + 20 = 40 → 4. The entry of the tail M = D + E = 20 + 4 = 24 → 6, the middle N = D + M = 20 + 6 = 26 → 8. A twenty in the bottom corner cannot come from reducing: the largest possible sum of the three numbers is 56, and none of the numbers from 23 to 56 has a digit sum above 13. So 6-8-20 has no backup sums, unlike 15-5-8 with its 26, 35, 44 and 53 — only 20. This was checked by running through every day from 1900 to 2100.
Five tails begin with the Lovers, and one more shares its centre and middle with 6-8-20. They are often confused:
The same arithmetic produces facts you will rarely see anywhere else:

ul: **It is a young tail.** Across all dates from 1900 to 2025, 6-8-20 comes up for about one date in forty-one (2.45%) — 15th place out of 26. But it is spread very unevenly. Among people born in the 1930s it is one in 126, in the 1960s one in 55, in the 1990s one in 32. Since 2000 it is every twentieth child (5%), and the tail climbs to eighth place. The reason is arithmetic: it needs a small sum. Twentieth-century years have a large arcanum (1984 → 22), and the sum of the three numbers almost always jumps past 20. Twenty-first-century years have a small arcanum (2004 → 6), and there is enough room for a twenty.

**In some years nobody has it.** If the year arcanum is between 19 and 22, the sum is already over 20 from the start. That is how four years in a row work out every nine years: 1954–1957, 1963–1966, 1972–1975, 1981–1984, 1990–1993. People born in these years cannot have the 6-8-20 tail. Since 1994 there has been no such gap, and there will be none until 2089.
**The most — 21 dates in a year.** These are the years with arcanum 6: 1959, 1968, 1977, 1986, 1995, 2004, 2013, 2022.

**It favours the start of the year.** The month number goes into the sum, and the bigger it is, the less room is left for the day and the year. Among people born in January, 6-8-20 is three times as common as among those born in December.

**People born on the 18th, 19th, 20th, 21st and 22nd never get it** — not in a single year from 1900 to 2100. The arcanum of such a day is already 18 to 22, which leaves too little for the month and the year. So it turns out that Judgement is never at the root for exactly those born on the twentieth. And the seventeenth gives this tail only once in two hundred years: 17 January 2000.

**20-8-6 is the same tail.** If you see 20, 8 and 6 on the bottom ray of your chart, you are reading the same tail from the outer corner to the centre. In this scheme there is no tail that begins with 20: the inner point M is always a multiple of three. The roles stay the same: the Lovers are the entry, Judgement is the root.

paragraphs: Popular readings explain the name with a legend about a past life. There are several versions. The soul supposedly broke with its family line: refused to carry on the ancestors’ work, followed its own desire and became an outcast. Or it faced a choice between love and duty to the family — and whichever side it sacrificed, it left resentment behind. In the darkest version it was treason or disobeying an order in war, which the family had to be ashamed of. And in this life the person supposedly feels like the black sheep among their own, waits for years for praise from their family and is torn between their own path and guilt. The legend cannot be checked: no one’s past can be reconstructed from a birth date. But as a metaphor it is accurate. This is how a person lives when any choice of their own feels like a small betrayal.

The name has a second side that is easy to miss. “Family Disappointment” can be read two ways: the family is disappointed in the person — and the person is disappointed in the family. Popular sites write about both: some about the one who “disgraced the family”, others about anger at parents and grievances that pile up for decades. The 6-8-20 tail really is about both sides. As you will see below, these are modes of one script, and a person often goes through both.

The word for “family” in the Russian name is rod — not the household but the lineage — and it rests on the root of the tail. In the popular tradition of the matrix the twentieth arcanum, Judgement, is called the arcanum of the lineage: ancestors, family memory, what is passed down. This link has support in Waite’s deck, and very visible support. On the twentieth card a man, a woman and their child between them rise from their tombs. Among the major cards of this deck, only here are a father, a mother and a child shown together. But next to this Waite makes a reservation that is almost never mentioned. He deliberately added more people to the card, beyond the three, **“as illustrating the insufficiency of current explanations”**. There is a family on the Judgement card, but the Judgement card is not only about family. For this tail that is the main key, and we will come back to it.

Even the “disgrace” of the second name turns up in Waite — in an unexpected place. In the divinatory list for the eighth card, Strength, come “power, energy, action, courage, magnanimity”, and at the end **“also complete success and honours”**. The reversed list ends with the words **“sometimes even disgrace”** — the very word of the tail’s second name. A calculated number is never reversed, and this article does not divide cards into “plus” and “minus”. But it is curious that the description of one card, the one in the middle of the tail, holds both poles of family judgement — honours and disgrace. In 6-8-20 the pride of the family and the disgrace of the family are not two different people but two ends of one axis, and the eight holds it.

And one last thing. There is a Russian saying that sounds like a ready-made verdict for this tail: v semye ne bez uroda — roughly, “every family has its black sheep”, literally “no family is without an urod”, a freak. The word urod is formed from rod, lineage, as is the verb uroditsya, “to be born a certain way”. And in Polish the related word uroda means “beauty”. One root gave disgrace in one language and beauty in another. For a tail where everything hangs on the family’s judgement, this is almost a parable: what to call disgrace and what to call beauty is decided by the eyes that are looking.

sections.h2: A family portrait at the beginning and at the end: how the circle works
paragraphs: In the first part of his book Waite goes through old designs of the cards, and one passage there sounds almost like a hint for this tail. He calls the Lovers of the eighteenth-century decks a card of married life: it shows **“father and mother, with their child placed between them”**, and the card is said to have been called Simulacrum fidei — “the symbol of conjugal faith”. When he reaches the twentieth card, Waite writes that on the surface it can only be the resurrection “of that triad—father, mother, child—whom we have met with already in the eighth card”. He described the family under number six, and number eight in his list is Strength, so this is most likely a slip of the pen. But it so happened that all three numbers of the tail met in one sentence about the twentieth card. **The 6-8-20 tail begins and ends with a family portrait.** The script is what happens in between.

**1. Entry: the Lovers — a choice that concerns more than just you.** Benebell Wen writes that in every traditional interpretation the Lovers is a card of moral choice, of choosing the right path. The male figure on it, according to Wen, is the mind, and the female figure is the heart, and the person has to choose between them. She compares this choice to Søren Kierkegaard’s “either/or”: to live for your own desire or by a sense of duty. And she adds that beneath it all lies a theme of indecision.

In 6-8-20 the choice immediately goes beyond one person. Whom to love, whom to marry, where to move, what to study, whether to baptise the child, whether to move closer to the parents — all of it concerns the family too, and the family is watching. Wen tells the Lovers and Justice apart by exactly this sign: the sixth card is a decision that involves the person themselves, the eleventh is a decision that involves the people who matter to them. For a person with this tail the line between them is erased. Any “I want” sounds to them like “I am against you”.

The same book, Either/Or, that Wen refers to contains a famous passage: “Marry, and you will regret it; do not marry, and you will also regret it; marry or do not marry, you will regret it either way.” In 6-8-20 this logic goes like this: choose what is yours and you disappoint them; choose them and you disappoint yourself. Someone will be disappointed whatever you do. So the choice is put off, made in secret, or made in one jerk, with a slammed door.

Waite, by the way, made on this very card the move that lies ahead for the tail. In his deck he removed the parents and the child from the sixth card and left two people, a man and a woman, **“unveiled before each other”**, like Adam and Eve in the first days of paradise. This, he writes, is “in all simplicity the card of human love”. A new family begins where two people choose each other, not where a council of elders has approved their choice. And there is one more detail of the picture that Wen points out: the man looks at the woman, and the woman looks up at the angel. On the sixth card only one person sees the angel.

**2. Mechanism: Strength — holding the choice by force.** Next comes the eight. On Waite’s card a woman is closing a lion’s jaws, and Waite specifies that in one of its aspects the lion signifies the passions. In this tail the lion is the very desire the Lovers woke up. Strength is the way of dealing with it. The history of the card holds a detail that describes the mechanism almost word for word. In the usual form the woman closes the jaws, but in the version printed by Court de Gebelin, in Waite’s words, “she is obviously opening it”. Waite thought the first version better symbolically, but either, he writes, is an instance of strength in its conventional understanding, the idea of mastery over the beast. A person with 6-8-20 has two ways as well.

The first is to **close the jaws.** Swallow your desire and stay the family’s pride. Study where you were told to, marry a “nice girl from our circle”, stay in your home town, keep the family business going. It takes a lot of strength, and from the outside it looks like a virtue: self-control, reliability, “everything rests on him”. The reward is the very “complete success and honours” from Waite’s list. Only these honours belong to someone else.

The second is to **open the jaws.** Defend the choice against everyone: leave, move away, stop calling, prove a point. This is Strength too — persistence, courage, the ability to bear the family’s coldness. But it is the strength of a roar, and it is aimed at the same place as in the first case — at the family. The person lives not their own choice but a war for it. Their life becomes a piece of evidence addressed to people who may long ago have stopped arguing about anything.

Wen explains why neither way works. The power of this card, she says, cannot be used as brute force: it works through gentle, subtle influence, and **“compassion is strength”**. And in the reversed meaning Wen names both extremes of the tail at once: the person is either “too stubborn and obstinate”, or holds back so much that they cannot reach their goal. True Strength in Waite is a third option. The lion on his card is already subdued and follows the woman on a chain of flowers. Waite explains this chain as **“the light burden”** of Divine Law, “when it has been taken into the heart of hearts”. The desire is neither swallowed nor set loose on the family. It walks beside you, and you can show it to others without frightening anyone.

The American psychiatrist Murray Bowen, the creator of family systems theory, has good language for this mechanism. His theory describes two ways of handling tension in the family of origin, both familiar to this tail. You can fuse: live by the family’s feelings and judgements as if you had none of your own. Or you can cut off: reduce contact to a minimum, move away, stop calling. Such an emotional cutoff, according to Bowen, gives only an illusion of independence: the tension does not disappear but looks for a new place. Closed jaws are fusion, open jaws are cutoff. Both positions rest on one and the same strength.

**3. Root: Judgement — a call that is answered from within.** In Waite the twentieth card is not about punishment. The angel blows the trumpet, the dead rise. It is, Waite writes, the accomplishment of the great work of transformation **“in answer to the summons of the Supernal—which summons is heard and answered from within”**.

Look at how the card is built. A man on the left, a woman on the right, a child between them — the same family as on the old Lovers. Only now the child stands with their back to us, facing the angel. And the parents look not at the child but in the same direction — upwards. All the figures, Waite writes, are “as one in the wonder, adoration and ecstacy” expressed by their attitudes. At a family court everyone looks at the accused. On the Judgement card nobody is glaring at anyone: everyone is listening to the trumpet.

This is the root task of 6-8-20. Not to leave the family and not to dissolve in it, but to stand among your own people — and hear your own call. The sixth card began with only one person seeing the angel. On the twentieth everyone hears it, and each answers for themselves. Russian has an exact word for this — prizvanie, “calling”, from the same root as zvat, “to call”. English keeps the same link: a calling is something that calls you. A calling is not chosen for approval and not taken up out of spite. It is heard.

Wen adds two thoughts that sound like release for a tail about “disgrace”. First: the person’s past, **“no matter how dark, no matter what”** they have done, is now behind them. Second: all the evidence is laid before the person, and they deliver the judgement themselves. And she describes reversed Judgement as an error of judgement: the person has misread the facts and reached a false conclusion. “I am the family’s disgrace” is exactly such a conclusion. It was drawn not from the facts of your life but from a family script that took shape long before you were born.

The most unexpected thing in Wen is said about Strength, the middle of the tail. In the sequence of the major arcana, Strength, she says, is a foreshadowing of what a person will need to reach Judgement and the World. **The mechanism of the tail is the very road to its root.** The same endurance that for years went into keeping silent or fighting is what you need to tell your family: “I have chosen this.” And to bear their answer.

Bowen has a name for this task too — differentiation of self: the ability to stay in contact with those close to you while holding your own position, especially under pressure. Not “they are right” and not “they are nothing to me”, but “I hear you — and I have decided otherwise”.

**4. Repetition.** As long as the root has not been lived, the circle repeats. Every new choice goes before the family court again: meeting the parents, changing profession, a wedding, the birth of a child, a move. And this tail has a feature that makes it so natural to call it a lineage tail: its roles are passed on. The one who was the “family’s disgrace” at twenty often says to their own children at fifty: “I’m disappointed in you.” The one who was the family’s pride demands the same from their own. Bowen called this multigenerational transmission: a family’s ways of handling anxiety pass from parents to children. The court is never dismissed — only its members change.
**Signs that the circle has gone round again:**

ul: the decision is made, but you put off the talk with your family “until the right moment”;
when you have good news, you first think about how to present it to your mother;
you do something so that “they see”, not because you want to;
a success nobody in the family has appreciated gives you no joy;
when asked “what do you want?”, you answer with what they do not want;
you catch yourself saying a parent’s phrase you promised yourself never to say.

paragraphs: Many people with 6-8-20 recognise all three modes in themselves — in different years. At school and university the person is the family’s pride: a medal, the “right” degree, photos in the family group chat. Closer to thirty, the outcast: a divorce the family did not accept, or a move after which the calls became rare. And later, with their own children or staff, the judge. The judge can also be inside. The person has long lived on their own, the parents may already be gone, but the verdicts still sound in their voice: “nothing will ever come of you”, “we put so much into you”. From the outside these are three different people. In fact they are one bottom ray of the chart.

A separate word about the Outcast. This is the most visible mode and the most deceptive. A break looks like freedom, but a person who spends years proving to their family that they are right is still standing before the family’s court — just in the place of the defence. The sign of a real way out is not the distance to the parents’ house but the fact that you no longer need anyone there to admit you were right.

sections.h2: Strength or Justice: a court with two instances
paragraphs: If you calculated your matrix in another calculator, you most likely saw Justice rather than Strength in the middle of this tail. There is no mistake here — there are two numberings of the deck. In the old Marseille order Justice is eighth and Strength eleventh, and most destiny matrix calculators follow that order. Waite swapped the cards “for reasons which satisfy myself” and added that the change would mean nothing to the reader. In this reading the eight is read according to Waite’s deck — as Strength.

But for 6-8-20 the second numbering explains a lot. Read the tail the way most calculators see it: the Lovers, Justice, Judgement. A choice — and then two courts in a row. No wonder the popular names of this tail sound like extracts from a court record: “disappointment”, “disgrace”, and in one of the tail lists, “development through justice”.

Wen clearly separates these two instances. Her Justice is **“human-made justice”**: the laws of man, not the laws of nature or the divine, the consequences of our decisions and actions. Judgement is awakening and epiphany, after which the person changes. The first instance weighs actions. The second wakes you up. The family court this tail is about is a court of the first instance: who is right, who owes whom, who let whom down. “We gave you everything, and you…” — “I never asked you to.” Both sides keep the ledger.

If your eight is Justice, the mechanism of the tail looks exactly like this: the choice is held not by force but by a ledger. Wen gives a precise description of how such a ledger goes bad. Reversed Justice, she says, is when **“what is fair will not feel fair”**: the person feels they have been treated unjustly. Then she notes the progression to the reversed Hanged Man — to martyrdom. Resentment of your family, saved up over years, makes a person a martyr of their own family. The number does not decide who is right in your family: real injustices happen too, and admitting them is not a weakness.

The two readings of the middle do not argue with each other. Strength answers how to hold your desire, Justice how to keep the ledger. And their root is shared — Judgement, which leads out of the first instance into the second: from the question “who is right?” to the question “what is calling me?” **While the family is working out who owes whom, nobody hears the trumpet.**

sections.h2: The hidden fourth card: everyone with 6-8-20 has the Emperor in the centre
paragraphs: Everyone with the 6-8-20 tail has 4, the Emperor, in the centre of the matrix. This is arithmetic: the sum of 20 plus the bottom corner of 20 gives 40, and 40 reduces to 4. The entry of the tail comes from the centre: the Lovers of this tail are made of Judgement and the Emperor, 20 + 4 = 24 → 6. What follows is our reading, not a rule of the method: here the choice of the heart is born where two voices meet — the call and the father’s law.

In this method the centre of the chart is the comfort zone, the state a person returns to when nothing is asked of them. The Emperor is a card of power and order. Wen writes that traditionally, in a man’s reading, it means self-mastery, and in a woman’s, a father figure, and that overall the card is **“the domination of the mind over the heart”**. Put this next to the Lovers, where the female figure is the heart and the male figure the mind. The entry of the tail is a choice of the heart; the comfort zone is the rule of the mind. So when the choice becomes too frightening, a person with 6-8-20 goes back to the throne: plans, order, duties, “I must”. Everything is under control, the decisions are reasonable, and nobody asks the heart.

The Emperor of this tail can be outside or inside. The outer one is the parental law that is obeyed: a father who “knows better”, the family code, the eldest of the line. The inner one is the person’s own throne, which they build after leaving: their own business, their own home, their own rules, where nobody tells them what to do. The Outcast often becomes the Emperor of their own kingdom — and builds it from the same blueprints they ran away from.

Wen has two images of the Emperor that this tail should know. The first is the landscape behind the throne: dry rocks, scorched earth. Wen asks what this ruler actually rules, what he has conquered. The kingdom is parched, and the dryness speaks of thirst — a thirst **“for a different kind of sovereignty than the one the Seeker has attained”**. The second image is King Midas. Everything he touched turned to gold, and he died of hunger: gold cannot nourish. And most tragic of all, Wen reminds us, he turned his beloved daughter to gold. For a tail about family disappointment it is hard to find a more exact image. A child loved as the family’s pride is a golden child. You can boast about them, but they are hard to hug.

Waite is restrained about the Emperor. He is “the power of this world”, “the lordship of thought”, but, Waite notes, not yet the wisdom that draws from a higher world. The father’s law is not the same as a call. So the key to 6-8-20 is the path from the centre to the root, from the throne to the trumpet. The Emperor says: “this is how it’s done.” Judgement asks: “what is calling you?” The first is needed to live an orderly life. The second, to live your own life.

sections.h2: A story that reads like this tail
paragraphs: There is a story that many read at school and few reread as adults — Pushkin’s “The Stationmaster”. The parallel with the tail is ours, not part of the method’s tradition. But there are too many coincidences to pass it by.

On the walls of the stationmaster Samson Vyrin hang pictures of the story of the prodigal son: “a venerable old man in a nightcap and dressing gown sends off a restless youth”, who carouses, herds swine, comes back and is forgiven. This is a script the family knows in advance. The stationmaster’s daughter Dunya leaves with a passing hussar. The coachman says she cried the whole way, **“though she seemed to be going of her own free will”**. This is the Lovers: the choice is made, and it does not come easily. The father walks to Petersburg to bring his “lost lamb” home. The hussar stuffs money into his cuff and shows him the door — the old man throws the banknotes on the ground and grinds them under his heel. Two days later he still makes his way to his daughter and finds her in luxury; seeing her father, she “fell on the carpet with a cry”, and he is thrown out again. After that the stationmaster lives by a verdict: “There are plenty of them in Petersburg, silly young things: today in satin and velvet, and tomorrow, you’ll see, sweeping the street with the tavern riffraff.” And he goes as far as saying something terrible: “you can’t help sinning and wishing her in her grave.”

Life did not follow the pictures on the wall. A few years later a carriage with six horses pulls up at the station: “a beautiful lady” with three small children, a wet nurse and a little black pug. By then the stationmaster has drunk himself to death. The lady goes to the cemetery. **“She lay down here and lay there a long time,”** a boy tells.

Compare this ending with the Judgement card. On the card the dead rise from their tombs, and the family rises together — father, mother, child. In Pushkin the child lies down on the father’s grave. This is Judgement turned inside out: the call is heard, but too late, and there is no one left to answer. The father judged his daughter by the pictures, not by her — Wen would call this a false conclusion from misread facts. The daughter never came while he was alive to tell him herself. Both held out, each on their own side. Only one thing was missing — a conversation while both were alive. That is exactly where the root of 6-8-20 lies.

sections.h2: Where else 4, 6, 8 and 20 appear in your chart
paragraphs: Since everyone with this tail has the same sum of the three numbers, many other points of the chart are the same too. Running through all dates from 1900 to 2025 gives this picture:

head: Where in the matrix
What everyone with 6-8-20 has
rows: Sky line (month — D — their sum), middle
22 if you were born from March to September; 4 in January and February; 13 from October to December

paragraphs: **Relationships.** Point M opens two triples at once: the tail and the relationship line M–R1–R. So for everyone with 6-8-20 the relationship line also begins with the Lovers. And for those born in years with arcanum 10 — 1900, 1999, 2008, 2017, 2026 — the relationship line repeats the tail entirely: 6-8-20. That is roughly one in nineteen people with this tail, for example 05.05.2008. For them the choice of partner and the family court are written into the chart twice.

**Manipura.** In Manipura, the chakra of will and independence, everyone with this tail has the Emperor twice, and Strength in the emotions column. Our reading: the will of this tail is made of the same material as its trap. Order and endurance are a real resource as long as they serve the choice rather than replace it.

**Purposes.** The options are this limited for a reason. When digits are added up, the remainder after division by 9 is preserved, and all four purposes are calculated from the same numbers of the day, month, year and bottom corner, whose sum is always the same for this tail. The most striking thing here is the social purpose. Almost everyone with 6-8-20 has there the same eight that holds the circle of the tail, although among all birth dates this happens for one in ten. What follows is our conclusion, not the books’. What works in the tail as holding — swallowing or defending — can ripen in dealings with people into real Strength: the skill of holding something strong gently, whether it is yours or someone else’s.

Almost two-thirds of people with this tail have the Fool, the twenty-second arcanum, as their personal purpose. Waite describes him as the spirit in search of experience and adds a detail that is hard to miss for this tail: the sun behind the Fool knows whence he came, whither he is going, and **“how he will return by another path after many days”**. Leaving in order to come back by another path is not a bad formula for a person who fears that any departure from the family is forever.

**Sixty years.** On the age scale the bottom corner D governs the years from 60 to 70, and everyone with this tail has Judgement there. This is the age at which a person usually becomes the eldest of the family line. The question of the tail comes back in a new role: who will you be for the younger ones — a judge or a trumpet? All of these are coincidences in the scheme, not a forecast and not information about health.
The scenes below are made-up examples, not a description of every person with this tail.

**A diploma for Dad.** He is thirty-four and a lawyer, like his father and grandfather. At family gatherings he is introduced as “our lawyer”, and he smiles. He has long been telling his wife he wants to quit and make furniture — “once Dad retires”. Dad has retired. Now it is “after his anniversary”. These are closed jaws: the desire has not gone anywhere, it is simply held down by force. And strength, as we remember, is something this tail has.

**A holiday once a year.** She lives in another city and comes to her parents for New Year. Two hours at the table and everything is back: “so when are the grandchildren coming?”, “and is that even a job?”. She leaves on the second of January instead of the fifth and decides on the train that she will not come again. These are open jaws. There is distance, but no freedom: the argument with the family goes on in her head the whole way.

**The family group chat.** Mum forwards a photo: her friend’s son has defended his dissertation. Not a word of reproach, just the photo. A person with 6-8-20 reads a verdict in it and walks around with a weight on them for half the day. Perhaps Mum just wanted to share. Perhaps not. The tail does not know what was on Mum’s mind. It knows something else: for this person, every message from the family passes through a courtroom.

The strong version in all three scenes is the same — to inform, not to ask permission. “Dad, I’m leaving the law and opening a workshop. I know you’ll be upset. It matters to me that you hear this from me.” The tail does not know how the conversation will end. Maybe with a month of coldness. Maybe in six months the father will come to look at the first table. But this is an answer to the trumpet, not to a verdict.
Everyone with 6-8-20 has a relationship line that begins with the same card as the tail — the Lovers. So in this tail love almost always passes through the question “what will they say at home?”

**A partner as an exam.** The Family’s Pride chooses someone who will pass the parents’ exam: from “our circle”, with a good profession, convenient for Sunday lunches. The Outcast chooses someone the family will certainly not accept — and the marriage becomes a fortress against the family. In both cases the choice is made not between two people but between a person and their family.

**Between mother and wife.** The most recognisable scene of this tail in marriage is the old family portrait in a new frame. The child between father and mother has grown up, and now they are an adult between their parents and their partner. “It’s me or your mother”, “whose family are we spending the holidays with?”, “why does she call every day?”. The same “either/or”, only from two sides at once. Wen, discussing the reversed Lovers, names meddling from an in-law outright. A calculated card is never reversed, and the number does not say whether your relatives meddle. But the theme itself is familiar to this tail.

The strong version here is a couple who decide together and speak to both families with one voice: “We’re seeing in the New Year at home. Come on the second.” The old name of the sixth card, “the symbol of conjugal faith”, means more in this tail than faithfulness to each other. It is faithfulness to your own choice in front of two families.

People with 6-8-20 often choose a profession in the family court: “we’re all doctors in this family”, “why on earth do you want design?”, “your father spent his whole life building this business”. The Family’s Pride takes the beaten path and puts up for years with work they did not choose. The Outcast chooses the opposite on principle and refuses any help so as not to owe anyone. Money from the family comes with conditions — “we gave you a flat, and you…” — and turns into a ledger of debts. This is the Justice of the second numbering: a ledger kept for years.

At work the same court moves into the boss’s office. A manager easily becomes an Emperor from whom you expect recognition rather than pay. Popular write-ups scare people with this tail with bosses who take credit for their work. The mechanism is simpler and needs no karma: when you work for honours, any praise held back feels like theft.

The strength here is real. People who have lived through 6-8-20 do well where the old and the new need to be joined. An heir who renews the family business instead of selling it or preserving it in amber. A specialist who helps people make decisions between duty and desire: family mediation, psychology, teaching, law. These are directions, not a list of professions: the choice is still made by interests and skills. The root of the tail suggests the main criterion — a calling, not approval.

Since 2000 this tail has gone to one child in twenty, so many parents read this section. The tail says nothing about your family and does not predict conflict. But if the script of the tail describes an adult who checks every choice against the family’s approval all their life, the most useful thing you can do is not to teach your child this.

ul: **Don’t turn your child into gold.** “I’m proud of you” and “I love you” are different phrases. The first is about achievements, the second is about the child. Say both, and say the second not only after the first.

**Don’t use shame.** “You’re disgracing us”, “what will people say”, “that’s not how we do things in this family” — these are the tools of the family court. A child with 6-8-20 will learn them faster than others and will then judge themselves with them for years.

**Allow small choices — and show that your disappointment is not fatal.** “I’m sorry you gave up music. I’ll live. Tell me what you like about football.” The child learns the main thing: you can choose what is yours, and the bond will not break.

**Don’t put them between you and the other parent.** Don’t ask whom they love more, and don’t complain to them about the other parent. The old family portrait with the child in the middle is exactly what this tail then spends a lifetime climbing out of.
**Ask “what draws you to it?”.** Not “why do you need that?”, but what exactly pulls them. This is how a child learns to hear their own trumpet and not only your judgements.

sections.h2: A calling or a verdict: how to tell them apart
paragraphs: **A calling or a verdict:**

ul: Whose voice does it speak in? If you can name the person and remember their intonation, it is a verdict, even when it sounds in your own head.
Does the thought pull you forward, towards something — or push you away, from something?
After it, do you have the energy to act — or the need to justify yourself?

paragraphs: **A choice or a reaction to the court:**

ul: Would you want this if your family never found out?
And if your family were delighted?
If you want it only in the first case, it is protest. If only in the second, it is honours. What is yours survives both questions.
Do you call your parents because you want to, or because otherwise things will be worse?
Can you turn down a family request without feeling that you have been expelled from the family?
Do you help out of love — or to settle the account?

paragraphs: **A boundary or a break:**

ul: A boundary says: “I don’t talk about this with you.” A break says: “I don’t talk to you.”
A boundary can be named out loud. A break usually happens in silence.
After a boundary the bond goes on. After a break, an argument stays in your head.

sections.h2: The tail in shadow and in light
paragraphs: “Minus” and “plus” here are not two kinds of people but two ways of using one and the same thing: a strong heart, great endurance and sensitivity to the family’s judgement.

sections.h2: What to do with the 6-8-20 tail: eight practices
paragraphs: These are the author’s exercises, derived from the logic of the triple — not a ritual and not a promise of results.

ol: **Find your own people in the family line.** Ask the older generation about those in your family who once did things their own way: moved away, married “the wrong person”, changed trade or faith. Almost every family has such a person, and a generation later they are often spoken of with pride. You are not the first to choose what is yours, and the family line has already lived through it.

**Inform, don’t ask permission.** A conversation about a decision is built from three phrases: “I’ve decided…”, “It matters to me that you hear this from me”, “I understand you may be upset, and I’m ready to talk about it”. A request for permission sounds different: “What do you think, may I…” The difference is who makes the decision.

**Two days for someone else’s disappointment.** When your family is disappointed, do nothing for two days: don’t justify yourself, don’t cancel the decision, don’t slam the door. Disappointment is another person’s feeling, not a verdict on you. It passes faster when it is neither smothered nor fanned. This is Strength on the chain of flowers: the lion is beside you, its jaws neither clamped shut by force nor opened to roar.

**Put a date on the verdict.** Write down the phrases that sound in your head in your family’s voices: “nothing will ever come of you”, “we did everything for you”, “that’s not how we do things in this family”. Next to each, note who said it, when and why. It often turns out the phrase was said once or twice, many years ago and about something else entirely. A verdict with a date stops being eternal.

**An inventory of the inheritance.** Three columns: what from your family you take with gratitude, what you leave with respect, and what you have not decided about yet. The 6-8-20 tail asks you neither to take everything nor to reject everything. It asks that you decide this, not your reaction to their judgement.

**Honours without an audience.** Once a month, write down what you are proud of yourself — things nobody in the family saw or would appreciate. If the list is empty, everything you do is addressed to the court.

**Don’t sit on the bench.** If you are a parent, a manager or an older sibling, replace “I’m disappointed in you” with a description: what happened, what you feel and what you want. “I’m sorry you dropped out of university. I’m worried about money. Tell me what you have in mind.” This is how the transmission across generations breaks: a family court cannot be dissolved by decree, but you can stop sitting on it.

**One sentence about the call.** Put into one sentence where you are drawn — not what is expected of you and not what you do not want. And take one small step in that direction each week. A calling rarely sounds like a trumpet. More often it is a quiet interest that does not go away for years.

paragraphs: If there is violence, threats or constant humiliation in the family, distance is not a failure of the tail and not a “betrayal of your lineage” but a normal form of protection. The root of 6-8-20 is about hearing your own call, not about putting up with anything for the sake of the bond.

sections.h2: The strength of 6-8-20: the person through whom something new enters the family
paragraphs: In the lived-through version this tail gives a rare combination. The person can choose with the heart and love seriously (the Lovers). They can bear someone else’s disappointment without breaking and without fighting (Strength). And they can renew themselves — not by burning the past but by raising it along with them (Judgement). Such people become translators between generations. Both a grandmother and a teenager can talk to them. They bring into the family a new person, a new profession, a new way of living — and the family does not split but grows. They are the first to say out loud what everyone kept quiet about, and after that it is easier to breathe in the house.

In the second part of Either/Or, Kierkegaard, speaking through Judge William, writes a sentence that suits this tail better than any spell: in choosing, it is not so much a question of choosing the right as of **“the energy, the earnestness, and the pathos with which one chooses”**. Even if a person chose wrongly, it is precisely through this energy that they will discover they were wrong. A person with 6-8-20 is afraid of choosing wrongly, because the family is watching. But what disappoints loved ones is not a mistake — it is the choice that was never made.

On Waite’s twentieth card it is not one child who rises but the whole family, and other people besides. Nobody looks at the child with reproach — everyone is turned towards the angel. This is 6-8-20 lived through: not a victory over the family and not a surrender to it, but a shared call that each person answers for themselves. The old family portrait was arranged around the child. The new one is arranged around the trumpet.

sections.h2: What this reading is based on

ul: **Calculation** — the classic destiny matrix scheme with points A–T: D = A + B + C, E = A + B + C + D, M = D + E, N = D + M; every sum over 22 is reduced by adding its digits. The “sum of exactly 20” rule, the constant centre of 4, and the years and days on which the tail never falls were checked by running through every day from 1900 to 2100 on the calculator engine. Frequencies, shares by decade and month, matches with the relationship line, chakras and purposes were calculated across all dates from 1900 to 2025.

**Card meanings** — A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1910, reissued 1922, illustrated by Pamela Colman Smith), and Benebell Wen, Holistic Tarot (2015). Both authors are quoted in their original English. The description of the old Lovers card, the “eighth card” in the passage on Judgement and Court de Gebelin’s open lion’s jaws come from Part I of Waite’s book; the word “eighth” was checked against a scan of the 1922 edition. The numbering follows Waite: VIII is Strength, XI is Justice.
**Kierkegaard** — Either/Or (1843): “marry, and you will regret it” from Part One, the words on the energy of choice from Part Two. Comparing the Lovers with Kierkegaard’s choice is Wen’s idea.
**Family systems theory** by Murray Bowen — the concepts of differentiation of self, emotional cutoff and multigenerational transmission.
**“The Stationmaster”** — A. S. Pushkin, The Tales of Belkin (1830); the quotations are our translation from the Russian text of the story.
**The word urod and Polish uroda** — after Krylov’s etymological dictionary.

**The names “Family Disappointment” and “Family Disgrace”, the past-life legend and the name “arcanum of the lineage” for the twentieth arcanum** come from popular readings of the destiny matrix. Neither Waite nor Wen wrote about the matrix or karmic tails: assembling the three cards into a script, the three modes, the reading of the centre, the parallel with Pushkin’s story and the practices are the author’s interpretation.

This is an esoteric model for self-observation, not a forecast and not a substitute for a specialist’s help. If there is violence, threats or addiction in the family, the problem is not the tail and not you: what is needed here is real help, not work with numbers.

faq.q: What happened in a past life to a person with the 6-8-20 tail?
faq.a: Popular readings speak of a break with the family line: the person supposedly abandoned the ancestors’ work, chose love over family duty or the other way round, became an outcast and brought disgrace on the family. Less often, treason or disobedience in war is mentioned. This is a legend of the tradition: neither numbers nor cards establish events of past lives. It is more useful to read it as a description of what is already visible now: the habit of living through each of your choices as a trial of yourself — or as a trial of your family.

faq.q: Does 6-8-20 mean that I am the family’s disgrace or that my family will turn away from me?
faq.a: No. The tail is three numbers derived from a birth date. It knows nothing about your family or how they feel about you, and it does not predict a break. It describes a way of living through choices that may repeat: feeling your family’s judgement too sharply. The name itself is more frightening than the script. Wen writes of the twentieth card that a person’s past, **no matter how dark**, is now behind them.

faq.q: Is it true that people with 6-8-20 have sick children and no luck in their careers?
faq.a: Popular write-ups contain frightening promises: children with serious illnesses, giving up a child, a boss who takes credit for your work. Neither the calculation nor the cards predict such events. Three numbers know nothing about your children’s health, and the birth of a child with special needs is not a punishment of the family line and not anyone’s fault. If the script of the tail touches on children at all, it does so very differently: it suggests not making them the family’s pride but loving them as they are.

faq.q: Do I need to make peace with my family and “work through my lineage”?
faq.a: The tail requires neither reconciliation at any cost nor a break. Its requirement is different: that decisions about your family be made by you, not by your reaction to its court. For some this will mean coming back, for others a calm distance without war. Ancestor rituals that some sites recommend can help you remember your lineage with gratitude, but they do not replace a real conversation with those who are alive. If there was violence or danger in the family, your safety matters more than any scheme, this one included.

faq.q: Why is 8 Strength in one calculator and Justice in another?
faq.a: These are two numberings of the deck. In the old Marseille order and in most matrix calculators the eighth card is Justice and the eleventh is Strength. Waite swapped them, and in his deck the eighth is Strength. The tail does not change because of this: the numbers are the same, only the name of the middle changes. How to read it under both numberings is covered in the section “Strength or Justice” above.

Yes, if 20, 8 and 6 are on the bottom ray of your chart: you have simply read the tail from the outer corner to the centre. In the calculation it is written from the inner point M to the corner D, and M is always a multiple of three, so there is no tail that begins with twenty. The roles do not change: 6 is the entry, 20 is the root.

faq.q: Are the 6-8-20 tail and the “6-8-20 program” the same thing?
faq.a: No. The karmic tail is only the triple on the bottom ray, between the centre and the bottom corner of the chart. The same numbers can appear on the relationship line M–R1–R — for roughly one date in two hundred and twenty. Most often this happens to people with a completely different tail, 6-5-17, for example 05.05.1987. There the triple describes not an old script but how you build closeness. People with 6-8-20 born in years with arcanum 10 (1900, 1999, 2008, 2017, 2026) have the triple in both places at once, and the practices in this article apply to both.

It shares its entry with 6-20-14 — the Lovers — and both tails have Judgement. But in 6-20-14 Judgement stands in the middle: there someone else’s voice holds the circle, and the root becomes Temperance, the skill of joining. In 6-8-20 Judgement is the root: a call you are yet to reach. With 15-8-11, 6-8-20 shares its centre, the Emperor, and its middle, Strength. The entry and the root differ: in 15-8-11 the circle begins with the Devil, craving, and ends with Justice. Put simply, 15-8-11 learns to direct power, while 6-8-20 learns to choose what is its own in front of the family.

faq.q: What does 6-8-20 mean in a compatibility matrix?
faq.a: In a compatibility matrix the numbers are calculated from both partners’ dates, and the triple there describes the couple’s shared script, not each person’s own tail. This reading is about the personal tail. If 6-8-20 comes up for a couple, its meaning can be read with the same key: the union is tested by whether the two can choose each other in front of two families and turn their marriage neither into an exam for the relatives nor into a fortress against them.

faq.q: Is 6-8-20 different for women and men?
faq.a: No. Sex plays no part in the calculation, and the meaning of the tail does not depend on it. It is easy to imagine the tail as the story of “a daughter who did not live up to expectations” or “a son who did not carry on his father’s work”, but these are stereotypes, not arithmetic. Anyone can be the Family’s Pride, the Outcast or the Judge — and most often it is one and the same person in different years.

The numbers in the matrix do not change — what changes is how the script plays out. Signs of a lived-through tail: you inform people of your decisions rather than ask permission; you bear someone else’s disappointment without justifying yourself and without war; the verdicts in your head have been given dates and have lost their eternity; you can name what you took from your family and say thank you for it; you do not pass verdicts on your own children. And most importantly: when asked “what do you want?”, you answer before you remember what they will say at home.

report: The 6-8-20 tail opens and closes on the same family portrait. Waite calls the Lovers of the eighteenth-century decks a card of married life, showing “father and mother, with their child placed between them”. Of the twentieth card, Judgement, he writes that on the surface it can only be the resurrection “of that triad—father, mother, child”. The six is the entry of the tail, the twenty its root. Between them is the story of a child who must finally choose for themselves.

Popular readings call this tail “Family Disappointment” and explain the name with a legend: the soul supposedly broke with its family line, refused to carry on the ancestors’ work, followed its own desire and became an outcast. The legend cannot be checked: a birth date reconstructs no one’s past. But as a metaphor it is accurate. **This is how a person lives when every choice of their own feels like a small betrayal.**

And the “disgrace” of the second popular name, “Family Disgrace”, comes from Waite himself — from his description of Strength, the eighth card and the middle of the tail. Its divinatory list ends with “complete success and honours”, the reversed list with “sometimes even disgrace”. A calculated number is never reversed, yet one card’s description holds both poles of family judgement. **The family’s pride and the family’s disgrace are not two different people but two ends of one axis**, and the eight holds it.

report.h3: Swallow the wish or fight for it — the same strength either way

report: Benebell Wen calls the Lovers a card of moral choice and likens the choice to Kierkegaard’s “either/or”. Kierkegaard has a famous line: “Marry, and you will regret it; do not marry, and you will also regret it.” In 6-8-20 it sounds like this: choose one’s own way and disappoint the family; choose the family’s and disappoint oneself. So the choice is put off, made in secret, or made in a rush, slamming the door.

Strength holds the circle. On Waite’s card a woman closes a lion’s jaws, and in one aspect, Waite says, the lion signifies the passions. In the version printed by Court de Gebelin, “she is obviously opening it”. A person with this tail has the same two gestures.

Closing the jaws means swallowing the desire and staying the family’s pride: enrolling where told, marrying a “nice girl from our circle”. The reward is that very “complete success and honours”. Only the honours belong to someone else.

Opening the jaws means defending the choice against everyone: walking out, moving away, not calling, proving a point. This is Strength too, but the strength of a roar, and it is aimed at the same target — the family. Life becomes evidence addressed to people who may have stopped arguing long ago.

report.h3: The Family’s Pride, the Outcast, the Judge — one person at different ages

report: At school the person is the family’s pride: a medal, the “right” degree, photos in the family group chat. Closer to thirty, the outcast: a divorce the family did not accept, or a move after which the calls became rare. Later, with children of their own, the judge. The one who was the “family’s disgrace” at twenty often tells their own children at fifty: “I’m disappointed in you.” **The court is never dismissed — only its members change.**

Everyone with 6-8-20 has the Emperor in the centre of the matrix, the comfort zone. When the choice grows too frightening, the person goes back to the throne: plans, order, duties, “I must”. For Wen this card is “the domination of the mind over the heart”, and she recalls King Midas, who turned his beloved daughter to gold. A child loved as the family’s pride is a golden child. **Such a child is easy to boast about and hard to hug.**

Pushkin’s “The Stationmaster” shows the price of this court — the parallel is ours, not the method’s tradition. The stationmaster’s daughter Dunya leaves with a hussar and cries the whole way, “though she seemed to be going of her own free will”. Her father lives by a verdict and even says something terrible: “you can’t help sinning and wishing her in her grave.” A few years later “a beautiful lady” drives up to the station with three small children. By then the stationmaster has drunk himself to death. “She lay down here and lay there a long time,” says a boy. On Waite’s Judgement card the family rises from the tombs together; in Pushkin the child lies down on the father’s grave: the call is heard, but there is no one left to answer. Only one thing was missing — a conversation while both were alive.

In Waite the twentieth card is not about punishment. The angel blows the trumpet, and the dead rise “in answer to the summons of the Supernal—which summons is heard and answered from within”. It is the same family, but the child faces the angel, and the parents look the same way — upwards. At a family court everyone looks at the accused. Here everyone listens to the trumpet. Russian has an exact word for this — prizvanie, “calling”, from zvat, “to call”. A calling is not chosen for approval and not taken up out of spite. It is heard.

Wen calls Strength a foreshadowing of what it will take to reach Judgement. **The mechanism of the tail is the very road to its root.** The same endurance that for years went into keeping silent or fighting is what it takes to tell the family: “I have chosen this.” And to bear their answer.

In Waite the subdued lion follows the woman on a chain of flowers — “the light burden” of Divine Law, “when it has been taken into the heart of hearts”. The desire is neither swallowed nor set loose on the family. In life it looks like this:

ul: inform rather than ask permission: “Dad, I’m leaving the law and opening a workshop. I know you’ll be upset. It matters to me that you hear this from me”;
when the family is disappointed, do nothing for two days: no justifying, no cancelling the decision, no slamming the door. Disappointment is another person’s feeling, not a verdict;
write down the phrases that sound in the head in the family’s voices, and next to each, who said it, when and why: a verdict with a date stops being eternal.

report: If there is violence, threats or constant humiliation in the family, distance is not a failure of the tail and not “renouncing the lineage” but normal protection. What is needed here is real help, not work with numbers.

report.h3: Through this person, something new enters the family

report: A person who has lived through 6-8-20 can choose with the heart, bear someone else’s disappointment without breaking and without fighting, and renew themselves without burning the past. Such people bring into the family a new person, a new profession, a new way of living — and the family does not split but grows. The fear of this tail is choosing wrongly with the family watching. But what disappoints loved ones is not a mistake — it is the choice that was never made.
The old family portrait the tail begins with was arranged around the child. The new one is arranged around the trumpet.
